In triglycerides (fats and oils), long carbon chains known as fatty acids may contain double bonds, which can be in

either the cis or trans configuration, as Figure 2.25 illustrates. Fats with at least one double bond between carbon atoms are unsaturated fats. When some of these bonds are in the cis configuration, the resulting bend in the chain's carbon backbone means that triglyceride molecules cannot pack tightly, so they remain liquid (oil) at room temperature. Alternatively, triglycerides with trans double bonds (popularly called trans fats), have relatively linear fatty acids that are able to pack tightly together at room temperature and form solid fats. In the human diet, trans fats are linked to an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, so many food manufacturers have reduced or eliminated their use in recent years. In contrast to unsaturated fats, we call triglycerides without double bonds between carbon atoms saturated fats, meaning that they contain all the hydrogen atoms available. response.answer_text: A fatty acid whose hydrocarbon chain has only single bonds between neighboring carbons is saturated, because the textbook defines a saturated fatty acid as one with only single bonds between neighboring carbons in the hydrocarbon chain, so that hydrogen atoms attached to the carbon skeleton are maximized [ev_008] [ev_001]. A fatty acid whose hydrocarbon chain has two carbon-carbon double bonds is unsaturated, since the textbook states that when the hydrocarbon chain contains a double bond the fatty acid is unsaturated [ev_008]; having more than one double bond is described as polyunsaturated [ev_008]. An unsaturated fatty acid does not have to contain exactly one double bond: it may have one or more double bonds in the hydrocarbon chain [ev_002] [ev_008]. Fats are described as a stored form of energy [ev_002], and phospholipids comprise the membrane's matrix [ev_002] [ev_003].
